```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 6.5, fig.height = 4.5,
                      dev = "svglite", fig.ext = "svg", dev.args = list(pointsize = 14),
                      eval = requireNamespace("ggplot2", quietly = TRUE))
options(knitr.kable.NA = "")
```

This article runs the whole cleaning workflow on a table shaped like a GBIF download: flag every record with all the tests its columns allow, look at what each test caught, and then compare several cleaning rules over the same flags before choosing one. The data are simulated so that every error is known, which makes it possible to check that each test catches what it should and nothing else. Installation is covered in [Get started](OccurrenceCleaner.html).

## Example data

The table has 2,276 records in GBIF's lower-case Darwin Core column names (`decimallongitude`, `countrycode`, `basisofrecord`, ...), which `occ_columns()` matches without renaming. Of these, 2,000 are background records drawn at random inside a box over each of five European countries, with that country's code. The boxes follow the borders only roughly: two of the Austrian points fall across the border in Bavaria, and the country test will say so.

The other 276 records carry planted errors, labelled in a column `truth` so the flags can be checked against it afterwards: herbarium sheets georeferenced to the capital where they are kept, coordinates typed as zeros, the GBIF headquarters in Copenhagen as a default location, swapped and negated coordinates, coordinates entered at whole degrees, botanic-garden specimens and cultivated plants, and 40 exact copies of background records.

<details>
<summary>Simulation code</summary>

```{r data-clean}
library(OccurrenceCleaner)
library(ggplot2)

set.seed(42)
boxes <- data.frame(code = c("AT", "DE", "FR", "ES", "PL"),
                    lon0 = c(13.0, 9.0, 1.0, -6.0, 17.0), lon1 = c(15.5, 12.0, 4.0, -4.5, 21.0),
                    lat0 = c(47.0, 49.5, 45.5, 38.0, 50.5), lat1 = c(48.0, 51.5, 47.5, 40.0, 52.0))
n <- 2000
b <- boxes[sample(nrow(boxes), n, TRUE), ]
spp <- c("Quercus robur", "Fagus sylvatica", "Bufo bufo", "Lucanus cervus", "Amanita muscaria")
occ <- data.frame(
  gbifid = as.character(seq_len(n)),
  species = sample(spp, n, TRUE),
  decimallongitude = round(runif(n, b$lon0, b$lon1), 5),
  decimallatitude = round(runif(n, b$lat0, b$lat1), 5),
  countrycode = b$code,
  year = sample(c(1850:2024), n, TRUE, prob = seq(0.2, 3, length.out = 175)),
  coordinateuncertaintyinmeters = sample(c(NA, 10, 30, 100, 1000, 5000), n, TRUE),
  basisofrecord = sample(c("HUMAN_OBSERVATION", "PRESERVED_SPECIMEN"), n, TRUE, c(0.8, 0.2)),
  establishmentmeans = NA_character_,
  issue = "")
occ$kingdom <- ifelse(grepl("Quercus|Fagus", occ$species), "Plantae",
                      ifelse(occ$species == "Amanita muscaria", "Fungi", "Animalia"))
```

```{r data-errors}
err <- function(k, truth, lon, lat, code, ...) {
  d <- occ[sample(n, k), ]
  d$gbifid <- paste0(truth, "-", seq_len(k))
  d$decimallongitude <- lon; d$decimallatitude <- lat; d$countrycode <- code
  extra <- list(...)
  for (nm in names(extra)) d[[nm]] <- extra[[nm]]
  d$truth <- truth
  d
}
occ$truth <- "background"
capitals <- data.frame(lon = c(16.37, 2.35, -3.70, 13.40, 21.01), lat = c(48.21, 48.86, 40.42, 52.52, 52.23),
                       code = c("AT", "FR", "ES", "DE", "PL"))
k <- sample(5, 60, TRUE)
bad <- rbind(
  err(60, "capital", capitals$lon[k] + rnorm(60, 0, 0.01), capitals$lat[k] + rnorm(60, 0, 0.01),
      capitals$code[k], basisofrecord = "PRESERVED_SPECIMEN", year = sample(1850:1950, 60, TRUE)),
  err(20, "zero", 0, 0, NA),
  err(15, "gbif_hq", 12.58, 55.67, "DK"),
  err(25, "swapped", occ$decimallatitude[1:25], occ$decimallongitude[1:25], occ$countrycode[1:25],
      issue = "PRESUMED_SWAPPED_COORDINATE"),
  err(25, "negated", -occ$decimallongitude[occ$countrycode == "FR"][1:25],
      occ$decimallatitude[occ$countrycode == "FR"][1:25], "FR"),
  err(30, "rounded", round(occ$decimallongitude[1:30]), round(occ$decimallatitude[1:30]),
      occ$countrycode[1:30], coordinateuncertaintyinmeters = NA),
  err(20, "living", occ$decimallongitude[31:50], occ$decimallatitude[31:50], occ$countrycode[31:50],
      basisofrecord = "LIVING_SPECIMEN"),
  err(21, "cultivated", occ$decimallongitude[51:71], occ$decimallatitude[51:71],
      occ$countrycode[51:71], establishmentmeans = "CULTIVATED"),
  err(20, "fuzzy_taxon", occ$decimallongitude[72:91], occ$decimallatitude[72:91],
      occ$countrycode[72:91], issue = "TAXON_MATCH_FUZZY;COORDINATE_ROUNDED"))
dups <- occ[sample(n, 40), ]; dups$gbifid <- paste0("dup-", 1:40); dups$truth <- "duplicate"
occ <- rbind(occ, bad, dups)
```

</details>

One record of each kind, and the size of each group:

```{r data-preview}
cols <- c("gbifid", "species", "decimallongitude", "decimallatitude", "countrycode", "issue", "truth")
occ[match(c("background", "capital", "swapped"), occ$truth), cols]
table(occ$truth)
```

The `issue` column lists GBIF's issue names separated by `;`, which is how both the simple-format download and the snapshot read through [vectra](https://gillescolling.com/vectra/) deliver them; a list column of character vectors works too.

## Flagging with every test the columns allow

Without `tests`, `flag_occurrences()` runs every test whose columns are in the table. Running a test only adds its flags; which records to exclude is chosen later, as a cleaning rule. `occ_columns()` only needs to be told the identifier, since the other defaults match case-insensitively:

```{r flag}
f <- flag_occurrences(occ, columns = occ_columns(id = "gbifid"))
dim(f)
```

`test_plan()` lists the tests that ran and the reason each other test did not. The table has coordinates, a species, a country code and the three GBIF fields, so the coordinate, GBIF and species outlier tests run. The fossil tests, the dataset tests, the habitat tests and the range test need columns or range polygons the table does not have; the articles on [fossils](fossils.html), on [outliers and dataset tests](outliers.html) and on [custom reference points and polygons](gazetteers.html) cover them:

```{r plan}
p <- test_plan(f)
all_tests <- p$test[p$run]
all_tests
p[!p$run, c("test", "missing")]
```

The result is the input with an integer `flags` column and one logical column per test. A `FALSE` in a flag column means that the test did not flag the record. It does not mean that every test examined the record: a test that did not run has no column, and a grouped test leaves a species with too few records untested. `flag_reference()` returns the label of the reference data that produced the flags, with the version of every layer. It is worth storing next to any cleaned table that goes into an analysis.

<details>
<summary>The full reference label</summary>

```{r reference}
flag_reference(f)
```

</details>

`summary()` turns the flags into shares per test. With one rule of every test, it gives for each test the records it flags, their percentage, and the records for which it is the only flag:

```{r counts}
s <- as.data.frame(summary(f, rules = list(all = all_tests)))
shown <- s[s$flagged > 0, c("test", "flagged", "pct", "only")]
```

```{r counts-table, echo = FALSE}
knitr::kable(shown, digits = 2, row.names = FALSE)
```

The `(any)` row is the rule as a whole: 274 of the 2,276 records carry at least one flag. The `only` column counts the records flagged by that test alone. These are the records the rule would additionally keep if that test were dropped from it.

Because the errors are labelled, a cross table of tests against the truth shows which test catches which kind of error, and whether any background record is flagged. Tests are in rows and the error groups in columns; the duplicates and the fuzzy taxon matches are left out, since one test each catches them:

```{r truth-table}
show <- c("zero", "equal", "capital", "centroid", "institution", "gbif_headquarters", "sea",
          "country_mismatch", "duplicate", "issue_coordinate", "basis_living", "establishment_managed")
groups <- c("background", "capital", "zero", "gbif_hq", "swapped", "negated", "rounded",
            "living", "cultivated")
tab <- sapply(show, function(t) tapply(f[[paste0("flag_", t)]], f$truth, sum))
tab <- t(tab[groups, ])
```

```{r truth-table-shown, echo = FALSE}
knitr::kable(tab)
```

Most error types trip more than one test. All 25 swapped records fail `country_mismatch` and carry GBIF's own `PRESUMED_SWAPPED_COORDINATE` warning (`issue_coordinate`); 9 of them also land at sea. The 15 GBIF-headquarters records are flagged by `gbif_headquarters` and `capital` (Copenhagen is within 10 km), and by `country_mismatch`, because the point lies just off the 1:50 million Natural Earth coastline of Denmark that the country test uses, while the 1:110 million land of the `sea` test still covers it. The zero coordinates fail `zero`, `equal`, `sea` and `country_mismatch`.

```{r truth-counts, include = FALSE}
neg_caught <- sum(rowSums(as.data.frame(f[f$truth == "negated", paste0("flag_", show)])) > 0)
```

The negated longitudes show the limit of the spatial tests. Only `r neg_caught` of 25 are caught: a French record at 1.5 E negated to 1.5 W is still in western France, on land and in the right country, and no record test can tell it from a correct one. Of the 30 records entered at whole degrees, five are caught by `centroid`, because they fall on the whole-degree country centroids of France (2 E, 46 N) and Germany (9 E, 51 N), and one by `institution`. The others are not caught: a whole-degree point in Austria is still in Austria, and GBIF's `COORDINATE_ROUNDED` warning does not mark them, since it records that GBIF itself rounded a coordinate to five decimals. Low precision of this kind is read from `coordinateuncertaintyinmeters` when the source states it; these 30 records state none.

Of the 2,000 background records, 1,998 carry no flag in these columns. The other two are the points in Bavaria, at 13.0 E, 47.6 to 47.7 N, and `country_mismatch` is right about them. The duplicates among the injected groups (7 cultivated, 7 living, 10 at the GBIF headquarters) arise because those records copy the coordinates of existing records and sometimes draw the same species.

## Where the flagged records are

`plot()` with `type = "map"` draws the records over the Natural Earth land, coloured by whether a rule removes them. With the CoordinateCleaner-equivalent spatial tests as the rule, the capital clusters, the point at (0, 0), the swapped records in Arabia and East Africa and the negated ones in the Atlantic stand out:

```{r map, fig.height = 5}
spatial <- c("zero", "equal", "capital", "centroid", "institution", "gbif_headquarters",
             "sea", "country_mismatch")
plot(f, type = "map", rules = list(spatial = spatial))
```

## How often tests coincide

A record is removed by a rule when it carries any test of that rule, so the overlap between tests decides how much each extra test adds. The flag word makes the combinations easy to count: each distinct value of `flags` is one combination of tests.

```{r combos}
flagged <- f[f$flags != 0L, ]
combo <- vapply(flagged$flags, function(w)
  paste(all_tests[vapply(all_tests, function(t) has_flag(w, t), logical(1))], collapse = " + "),
  character(1))
knitr::kable(head(sort(table(combo), decreasing = TRUE), 12), col.names = c("tests", "records"))
```

The most common combination is `capital + urban`: a capital lies inside its own urban area, so in a rule that already includes `capital`, adding `urban` removes only the city records more than 10 km from the capital point. Of the 20 zero-coordinate records, 15 carry seven tests at once: `zero`, `equal`, `sea`, `country_mismatch`, `outlier`, `aohi` (the inventory has a point at (0, 0)) and `duplicate`, since they share their coordinates and often their species. The swapped records lie far from the other records of their species, so `outlier` flags all 25 of them. Records with a single flag (`duplicate`, `issue_rounded`, `establishment_managed`, `basis_living`) are the ones a rule keeps or loses depending on whether that one test is in it.

## Comparing cleaning rules

A cleaning rule is a set of tests. Five rules, from loose to strict, show the range of choices on the same flags:

- `coordinatecleaner`: the [CoordinateCleaner](https://ropensci.github.io/CoordinateCleaner/) defaults of `clean_coordinates()` without the outlier test (invalid, zero, equal, capital, centroid, institution, GBIF headquarters, sea), the same rule as in [Choosing a cleaning rule](rules.html);

- `coordinatecleaner_country`: `coordinatecleaner` plus the country check;

- `coordinatecleaner_gbif`: `coordinatecleaner_country` plus GBIF's coordinate and taxon warnings;

- `wild`: `coordinatecleaner_gbif`, and also excludes living specimens and cultivated or managed individuals;

- `strict`: every test, including duplicates and GBIF's rounding note.

```{r rules}
rules <- list(
  coordinatecleaner = c("invalid", "zero", "equal", "capital", "centroid", "institution",
                        "gbif_headquarters", "sea"))
rules$coordinatecleaner_country <- c(rules$coordinatecleaner,
                                     "country_mismatch")
rules$coordinatecleaner_gbif <- c(rules$coordinatecleaner_country,
                                  "issue_coordinate", "issue_taxon")
rules$wild <- c(rules$coordinatecleaner_gbif,
                "basis_living", "establishment_managed")
rules$strict <- all_tests
t_all <- as.data.frame(tally_flags(f, rules = rules))
ladder <- data.frame(rule = names(rules), tests = lengths(rules),
                     removed = unlist(t_all[1, paste0("removed_", names(rules))], use.names = FALSE),
                     kept = unlist(t_all[1, paste0("kept_", names(rules))], use.names = FALSE))
ladder$added <- c(ladder$removed[1], diff(ladder$removed))
```

```{r rules-table, echo = FALSE}
knitr::kable(ladder, row.names = FALSE)
```

The ladder removes 125 records under `coordinatecleaner` and 274 under `strict`. The country check adds 21, the GBIF warnings 20 and the living and cultivated records 41. `strict` adds the remaining 67 through `duplicate` (42 records, 40 of them the injected copies), `urban` (20) and `aohi` (6), some records carrying more than one; the 20 records with `issue_rounded` are already removed through `issue_taxon`.

For one rule, `plot()` on the summary draws a bar per test: the full bar is the share the test flags, the dark part the share for which it is the only reason the rule removes the record. A test with a long light bar and a short dark one mostly flags records that other tests in the rule remove anyway. `invalid` is 0 here because every example record has valid coordinates:

```{r rule-bars, fig.height = 6}
plot(summary(f, rules = rules["coordinatecleaner_gbif"]))
```

`tally_flags()` returns `removed_<rule>` and `kept_<rule>` for every rule, plus `flagged_<test>` for every test, per group. Grouped by kingdom it shows whether a rule hits one group harder than another. The share of each kingdom's records that each rule removes, rules in rows:

```{r rules-kingdom}
t_k <- as.data.frame(tally_flags(f, by = "kingdom", rules = rules))
share <- sapply(names(rules), function(r) round(t_k[[paste0("removed_", r)]] / t_k$n, 3))
dimnames(share) <- list(t_k$kingdom, names(rules))
```

```{r rules-kingdom-table, echo = FALSE}
knitr::kable(t(share))
```

The same table as a figure, one line per kingdom across the rule ladder:

```{r rules-plot, fig.height = 3.8}
long <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(rules), function(r)
  data.frame(kingdom = rownames(share), rule = r, share = share[, r])))
long$rule <- factor(long$rule, levels = names(rules))
kingdom_cols <- c(Animalia = "#B5342B", Fungi = "#2E6F9E", Plantae = "#3F7A3D")
ggplot(long, aes(rule, share, colour = kingdom, shape = kingdom, group = kingdom)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) + geom_point(size = 2.5) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = kingdom_cols) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = function(v) paste0(100 * v, " %")) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "records removed") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 17) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 35, hjust = 1),
        panel.background = element_rect(fill = "transparent", colour = NA),
        plot.background = element_rect(fill = "transparent", colour = NA),
        legend.background = element_rect(fill = "transparent", colour = NA))
```

## Record age and coordinate uncertainty

Year and stated coordinate uncertainty are not tests. They stay raw columns and are cut into bins at tally time, so the same flags support any age or precision threshold. Grouping by year bin shows where a rule removes most:

```{r year-bins}
t_y <- tally_flags(f, bins = list(year = c(1900, 1950, 2000)),
                   rules = rules["coordinatecleaner_country"])
t_y$share <- round(t_y$removed_coordinatecleaner_country / t_y$n, 3)
shown <- t_y[, c("year_bin", "n", "flagged_capital", "removed_coordinatecleaner_country", "share")]
```

```{r year-bins-table, echo = FALSE}
knitr::kable(shown, col.names = c("year", "n", "flagged by capital", "removed", "share"))
```

The rule removes 13.9 % of the records before 1900 and 3.2 % of those from 2000 on, because the capital-georeferenced herbarium sheets were simulated with years before 1950. Uncertainty bins work the same way; records without a stated uncertainty form the group `"missing"`:

```{r unc-bins}
t_u <- tally_flags(f, bins = list(coordinateuncertaintyinmeters = c(100, 1000)),
                   rules = rules["coordinatecleaner_country"])
shown <- t_u[, c("coordinateuncertaintyinmeters_bin", "n",
                 "removed_coordinatecleaner_country", "kept_coordinatecleaner_country")]
```

```{r unc-bins-table, echo = FALSE}
knitr::kable(shown, col.names = c("uncertainty (m)", "n", "removed", "kept"))
```

A threshold on uncertainty is then a filter on the raw column next to the rule, for example keeping records with a stated uncertainty of at most 1 km:

```{r cut}
kept <- keep_unflagged(f, rules$coordinatecleaner_country)
kept <- kept[which(kept$coordinateuncertaintyinmeters <= 1000), ]
c(records = nrow(f), kept = nrow(kept))
```

## The cleaned table

Applying a rule is one call to `keep_unflagged()`. The flags stay attached, so a later analysis can still tell which tests the kept records passed and can tighten the rule without rerunning anything:

```{r apply}
clean <- keep_unflagged(f, rules$wild)
nrow(clean)
table(clean$truth)
```

The `wild` rule keeps 1,998 of the 2,000 background records and removes every injected error except the 40 duplicates, which it does not target, and 24 of the 30 whole-degree records and the 7 negated records, which no record test can see. The 20 records with a fuzzy taxon match are removed through `issue_taxon`, although their coordinates are fine.

## Practical guidance

- **Run every test the columns allow.** `flag_occurrences()` does so without `tests`, and `test_plan()` shows what did not run and why. The pass over the records is the expensive step; rules are a bit-mask query afterwards. On an AMD Ryzen 7 5700G the nine CoordinateCleaner tests that need only coordinates and a species took 1.9 s for one million records in memory (see the timings in [Compatibility with CoordinateCleaner](coordinatecleaner.html#timings)).

- **`country_mismatch` needs a country code and flags records without one.** A record with no code, or one that falls at sea, is flagged, as in [CoordinateCleaner](https://ropensci.github.io/CoordinateCleaner/). In a GBIF table where many records lack `countrycode`, that test alone can flag a large share; the tally per test shows it before it goes into a rule.

- **`sea` depends on the land scale.** The default 1:110 million land is coarse: in the example the GBIF headquarters are on land at that scale and at sea on the 1:50 million coast. For coastal or island taxa, `land_scale = 50` or `10` changes the result for records within a few kilometres of the coast; [Reference data](reference-data.html) shows the size of the difference.

- **`duplicate` depends on what counts as the same record.** By default it is the same coordinates and the same `species` value. Adding `duplicate_by = "eventdate"` keeps repeat visits apart; `duplicate_cell = 0.1` treats records in the same 0.1-degree cell as duplicates, which suits a grid-based analysis. On streamed input the test compares records across all input files, as on a data frame.

- **GBIF issue tests are GBIF's own processing results.** They catch errors that the spatial tests cannot see (a swapped coordinate that still lands on land, a fuzzy taxon match). `issue_rounded` is a precision note rather than an error: GBIF sets `COORDINATE_ROUNDED` when it rounds a coordinate given with more than five decimals, which moves the point by at most about 1 m.

- **Do not cut at a threshold during flagging.** Year, uncertainty and any other numeric field belong in `bins` or in a subset after the rule, so one flag pass serves every threshold an analysis or a reviewer asks for.
